rw: A benefit is the advantage or value a customer gets from a feature, such as comfort or savings. Salespeople turn features into benefits because buyers purchase to meet needs.

ww.A characteristic of the product itself: This describes a feature, which is a physical or technical trait of the product itself, such as size, material or speed, rather than what it does for the buyer.
ww.The number sold in the last year: Sales volume is a performance figure for the business. It says nothing about what the product does for an individual buyer, so it is not a benefit.
ww.The cost of making the whole product: Production cost is an internal business figure. Buyers care about the value they receive, and cost of making the item does not describe any advantage to them.

rw: The part after 'so' explains what the padded strap does for the buyer: no sore shoulders. That customer advantage is the definition of a benefit.

ww.A close: A close is the step where the salesperson asks for the buyer's decision to purchase. The 'so it will not hurt' part explains value instead of asking for the sale.
ww.An objection: An objection is a concern the buyer raises against buying. Here the salesperson is making a positive point, not answering a buyer's worry or resistance.
ww.A feature: The feature is the padded strap, the physical characteristic of the backpack. The part after 'so' explains what that feature does for the user, which is the benefit.

rw: An objection is a concern or reason a buyer raises, such as price, quality or timing. Handling objections respectfully is a key step in the selling process before closing.

ww.A discount offered by the seller to the: A discount is a price reduction the seller offers. It is a selling tool, not a statement by the buyer, so it does not describe an objection.
ww.A question about the store's hours of bu: A question about store hours is routine information seeking and not a reason for refusing to buy, so it is not an objection to the product.
ww.A final agreement to buy the product, si: A signed agreement to buy is the result of a successful close. It is the opposite of an objection, which expresses hesitation before agreeing.

rw: Listening first shows respect and uncovers the real concern. Then the salesperson explains value and compares benefits to cost, which addresses a price objection without damaging trust.

ww.Argue that the customer is wrong about t: Arguing with the customer creates conflict and damages the relationship. Telling a buyer they are wrong about the price rarely persuades and often ends the sale.
ww.Lower the price at once without discussi: Cutting the price immediately skips the chance to show value and reduces profit. It also teaches the buyer that the original price was negotiable for no reason.
ww.Ignore the comment and keep talking abou: Ignoring the comment leaves the objection unresolved, so the buyer keeps worrying about price. Good salespeople acknowledge concerns instead of talking past them.

rw: Closing a sale means asking for the buyer's decision and completing the purchase. It is the stage after presenting benefits and handling objections, where the transaction is made.

ww.Ignoring the buyer's questions about the: Ignoring questions would frustrate the buyer and prevent a sale. Closing involves responding to concerns, not avoiding them, so this describes poor selling rather than a close.
ww.Ending a store's business for the day an: Locking up at the end of the day is a store closing procedure. In selling, 'closing' means getting the customer's purchase decision, not shutting the business.
ww.Hanging up after a phone call without a: Hanging up without a decision means the sale was not completed. Closing requires reaching an outcome with the buyer, usually by asking for the order.

rw: This is an alternative-choice close. It assumes the buyer will buy and only asks which item, moving the conversation from whether to buy toward which one.

ww.There is nothing else I can tell you tod: Saying there is nothing more to tell ends the conversation without asking for a decision. A closing technique must prompt the buyer to choose or commit.
ww.I will let you think about it for a few: Telling the buyer to take years to think gives away urgency and invites the sale to be lost. It does not guide the buyer to a decision.
ww.Please leave if you are not sure about i: Asking an unsure buyer to leave is rude and ends the sale. Closing techniques guide the buyer toward a purchase and do not push the customer away.

rw: Follow-up means contacting the customer after the sale to confirm satisfaction, solve problems and encourage repeat business. It builds loyalty and referrals that raise future sales.

ww.Avoiding contact with the buyer after th: Avoiding contact after the sale ignores the customer's needs and loses repeat business. Follow-up is the opposite: staying in touch to confirm the buyer is satisfied.
ww.Reducing the product's quality after the: Lowering quality after a sale would hurt customers and the company's reputation. It is unethical and has nothing to do with the follow-up step of selling.
ww.Raising the price after the sale is made: Raising the price after the sale would break the agreement with the buyer and destroy trust. Follow-up is about service and satisfaction, not changing terms.

rw: Suggestion selling means offering extra or related items that go with the main purchase, like batteries with a toy. It adds value for the customer and raises the sale total.

ww.Refusing to sell what the customer wants: Refusing to sell what the customer wants would lose the sale and has nothing to do with suggesting add-ons. It does not describe any selling technique.
ww.Selling only the cheapest item in the st: Selling only the cheapest item is a fixed pricing approach, not suggesting extra products. It ignores customer needs, which suggestion selling is meant to serve.
ww.Selling only to customers who ask for it: Waiting until a customer asks twice describes passive selling. Suggestion selling is proactive, because the seller offers related items without being asked.

rw: A memory card stores photos and a case protects the camera, so both are accessories the buyer will actually need. That makes this a helpful, relevant suggestion.

ww.A kitchen blender for home use: A kitchen blender does not relate to photography, so offering it would not help the camera buyer. Suggestions should complement the main purchase.
ww.A bicycle helmet for children: A child's bicycle helmet has no connection to using a camera. A helpful suggestion fits the item just bought, which this does not.
ww.A bag of garden soil for planting: Garden soil is unrelated to a camera purchase and would not meet any need the buyer has. Good suggestions match how the product will be used.

rw: Trading up means encouraging a customer to buy a more expensive, higher-quality version of an item. It benefits the customer through better features and raises the sale total.

ww.Encouraging a customer to return a produ: Encouraging a return for credit is a returns procedure, not selling. Trading up aims to increase the sale value, whereas returns reduce sales for the store.
ww.Encouraging a customer to buy a cheaper: Pushing a cheaper version is trading down, which lowers the sale amount. Trading up is the reverse: moving the buyer toward a higher-priced option.
ww.Encouraging a customer to leave the stor: Encouraging the customer to leave ends the sale and helps no one. Trading up is about guiding a buyer to a better, higher-priced product.

rw: Product knowledge means understanding a product's features, benefits and uses. With it, salespeople can explain value, answer questions and match items to needs.

ww.Knowing a competitor's private sales dat: A competitor's private data is not product knowledge and may be obtained unethically. Product knowledge concerns the seller's own products and how they serve customers.
ww.Knowing the store's opening hours and it: Store hours and address are general business information. They do not tell a salesperson what the product does, so this is not product knowledge.
ww.Knowing a customer's home address and ph: A customer's address and phone number are personal contact details and have nothing to do with knowing the product being sold.

rw: Knowing the product lets a salesperson answer questions with confidence, build trust and match the right product to the customer's needs, which leads to satisfied buyers and sales.

ww.To hide the product's drawbacks from the: Hiding drawbacks from buyers is dishonest and can be illegal. Strong product knowledge is used to inform customers truthfully, not to conceal problems.
ww.To make the sale last as long as possibl: Extending the length of a sale does not help the customer and wastes time. Product knowledge is meant to make selling efficient and useful, not longer.
ww.To avoid listening to the customer and w: Product knowledge should work together with listening. Ignoring what the customer wants leads to poor matches and lost sales, so this is the opposite of good practice.

rw: Relationship selling focuses on building long-term trust and repeat business with customers. It values ongoing satisfaction and loyalty over making a single quick sale.

ww.Selling only to family members and to cl: Relationship selling is not limited to family and friends. It applies to all customers by building trust over time, not by selling to people the seller already knows.
ww.Avoiding any follow-up after the sale is: Avoiding follow-up is the opposite of relationship selling, which depends on staying in touch after the sale to maintain trust and encourage repeat purchases.
ww.Making as many one-time sales as possibl: Maximizing one-time sales with no later contact is transaction selling. Relationship selling instead keeps in touch with customers to earn their repeat business over many years.

rw: Honest information, including a product's limits, respects the customer and builds trust. Ethical selling avoids deception and pressure, leading to satisfied customers and repeat sales.

ww.Pressuring buyers until they give in and: Pressuring buyers until they give in is manipulative and damages trust. Ethical selling respects the customer's right to make a free and informed choice.
ww.Hiding a product's problems to close the: Hiding a product's problems is deceptive and may violate consumer protection law. Ethical sellers disclose material information the buyer needs to decide.
ww.Making false claims to beat a competitor: False claims about competitors or products are dishonest and can lead to legal action for false advertising. Ethical selling relies on truthful statements.

rw: A sales quota is a target, in dollars or units, that a salesperson is expected to reach in a period. Managers use quotas to measure and reward performance.

ww.A discount given to every customer who c: A discount for every customer is a pricing policy. A quota is a goal set for the salesperson, not a price reduction given to buyers.
ww.A tax on each item that a salesperson se: A tax on items is a government charge, such as sales tax. A quota is an internal sales goal that has nothing to do with taxing items sold.
ww.A limit on how many customers can enter: Limiting how many customers enter a store is a capacity rule. A quota concerns the sales volume a seller is expected to achieve.

rw: Excess is $24,000 - $20,000 = $4,000. Dividing by the quota gives $4,000 / $20,000 = 0.20, or 20%, so the salesperson beat the quota by 20 percent.

ww.120%: 120% is the sales as a share of quota ($24,000 / $20,000 = 1.20). The question asks by how much they exceeded it, which is 120% minus 100%.
ww.4%: 4% might come from dividing $4,000 by $100,000 or a similar slip. The excess is $4,000 and the quota is $20,000, so the correct ratio is much higher.
ww.83%: 83% results from dividing $20,000 by $24,000 (0.833), which compares quota to sales. The excess must be measured against the quota, not against the sales.

rw: A commission is pay based on a percentage of the sales a person makes. It rewards effort, since earnings rise as the salesperson sells more.

ww.Pay that is a fixed yearly amount for a: A fixed yearly amount is a salary. Commission varies with performance, so a flat annual pay does not describe commission.
ww.Pay given as a gift at the end of the ye: A gift at year end is a bonus or present and is not tied to a percentage of sales, so it is not commission.
ww.Pay that is the same every hour worked e: Pay that is the same for every hour is a regular hourly wage. Commission changes with the sales produced, not with hours worked.

rw: Commission equals sales times rate: $15,000 x 0.06 = $900. This is the percentage of sales the salesperson earns as pay.

ww.$9,000: $9,000 is 60% of $15,000, a misplaced decimal point. A 6% rate means 0.06, so the commission must be much smaller than this amount.
ww.$90: $90 is 0.6% of $15,000 and results from moving the decimal one place too far. The 6% rate should be converted to 0.06 before multiplying.
ww.$2,500: $2,500 results from dividing $15,000 by 6, which is not how percent is calculated. Multiply the sales by 0.06 instead to get the commission.

rw: A needs assessment means asking questions to learn what the customer needs and wants. This lets the seller recommend the right product instead of guessing.

ww.Showing every product in the store to th: Showing every product does not identify needs and may overwhelm the customer. Needs assessment comes first, so the seller can show only suitable items.
ww.Telling the customer what they need with: Telling customers what they need without asking skips the assessment entirely. Good selling begins with questions and listening rather than assumptions.
ww.Printing a price list for the customer t: A price list does not discover the customer's needs. Needs assessment is an interactive questioning process, not handing out information.

rw: Budget and intended programs are key needs questions. They help the seller choose a laptop with the right price, power and software for school and travel.

ww.Whether they like the seller's shoes or: The seller's shoes or hairstyle have no link to the customer's needs. Questions should focus on how the customer will use the laptop.
ww.What their favorite food is at lunch tim: Lunch preferences do not help choose a laptop. The next question should clarify use, budget and features, not unrelated personal tastes.
ww.Where they went to elementary school and: A customer's elementary school and teachers are unrelated to selecting a laptop. Relevant questions concern budget, uses and needed features.

rw: An intermediary is a business such as a wholesaler or retailer between the producer and final buyer. It helps move goods, store them and sell them, forming part of the channel.

ww.A customer who buys goods directly from: A customer who buys direct from the factory is an end buyer, not a middle link. An intermediary stands between the producer and the final buyer.
ww.A company that supplies raw materials to: A raw material supplier sits before the producer in the supply chain, not between the producer and the consumer, so it is not a channel intermediary.
ww.A government office that sets the price: A government office that sets prices is a regulator and not part of the distribution channel. Intermediaries buy, hold or sell goods themselves.

rw: Disintermediation removes middlemen such as wholesalers or retailers so the producer sells directly to customers, often online. It can cut costs and give the producer more control.

ww.Raising the price of goods at every step: Raising prices at every step describes markup layering, not channel structure. Disintermediation specifically involves removing intermediaries from the channel.
ww.Adding more wholesalers to a distributio: Adding wholesalers adds layers to the channel, which is the opposite of disintermediation. The term refers to cutting out middlemen.
ww.Closing a factory to cut the cost of mak: Closing a factory to cut production costs is a manufacturing decision. Disintermediation is about distribution channel structure, not about production.

rw: Selling vegetable boxes straight to homes removes the grocery stores as intermediaries. That is disintermediation through a direct channel from producer to consumer.

ww.Channel conflict with its own retail out: Channel conflict is a dispute between channel members. The farm's box program may cause some, but the question asks what the direct delivery model itself is.
ww.Intensive distribution through every sto: Intensive distribution places a product in as many outlets as possible. The farm is cutting out stores to deliver itself, which is the opposite.
ww.A reverse channel for returned goods onl: A reverse channel handles returns, recycling or reuse of goods. The farm is delivering new vegetables to customers, not collecting used goods.

rw: Omnichannel retailing integrates stores, apps and websites so customers move between them smoothly, with shared inventory, accounts and order history across all of them.

ww.Selling only to other businesses in bulk: Selling only to other businesses in bulk is business-to-business wholesale. Omnichannel is a retail approach that connects many customer-facing channels.
ww.Selling only through one physical store: Using one location in a single city is the opposite of multiple integrated channels, so it cannot be omnichannel.
ww.Using several unrelated channels that do: Unrelated channels that share no data are multichannel at best. Omnichannel requires the channels to be connected so the customer experience is consistent.

rw: Ordering online, returning in a store and having the store see the order history shows linked channels. That connected experience is omnichannel retailing.

ww.Price skimming at launch: Price skimming sets a high initial price on a new product at launch. It has nothing to do with how orders and returns work across channels.
ww.Direct mail promotion: Direct mail promotion sends printed advertising to homes. The scenario concerns channel integration for orders and returns, not mailed ads.
ww.Exclusive distribution: Exclusive distribution gives one outlet the right to sell a product in an area. It does not describe sharing data between online and store channels.

rw: RFID tags use radio signals so goods can be scanned and located automatically during transport and storage, which improves inventory accuracy and reduces manual counting.

ww.Setting the final price shown in adverti: Prices are set by management decisions, not by radio frequency tags. RFID reads tags to identify items, so it does not decide what ads or shelves show.
ww.Choosing the color and shape of a packag: Package color and shape are design decisions. RFID tags track items but do not influence how packaging looks.
ww.Training sales staff to greet customers: Training staff to greet customers is a human resources task, not a function of tracking technology such as RFID.

rw: A barcode is scanned to identify a product quickly, so the system can look up its price and update stock records. It speeds checkout and improves tracking accuracy.

ww.Advertising a product on television and: Television and radio ads are promotion tools. A barcode is a printed code scanned at the register, which does not advertise anything.
ww.Showing customers how to use a product a: Instructions for using a product are given in manuals or demos. A barcode only stores a number that identifies the item.
ww.Protecting a product from copying throug: Protecting designs from copying is done through legal registration such as patents. A barcode does not provide legal protection.

rw: Each scan subtracts the item from stock, so inventory records stay current and accurate. This supports timely reordering and helps avoid shortages or excess stock.

ww.Higher prices for every customer in the: Scanning does not raise prices for customers. The system only records items, and prices are set by management decisions.
ww.Removal of the need to count stock by ha: Physical counts are still needed to check for theft, damage or errors. Automatic updates reduce counting work but do not remove the need entirely.
ww.Fewer products offered to customers in e: Scanning does not reduce the product range. It records what is sold, and that information can actually help a store stock the right goods.

rw: A cold chain is a supply chain that keeps perishable goods such as food and vaccines at controlled low temperatures from producer to consumer, preventing spoilage.

ww.A group of suppliers that refuse to work: Suppliers who refuse to cooperate on pricing is not a cold chain. The term refers to temperature control, not to supplier behavior.
ww.A rule that sets low prices in winter fo: A winter pricing rule is a pricing policy. A cold chain concerns refrigerated transport and storage, not seasonal prices.
ww.A chain of ice cream shops spread across: A chain of ice cream shops is a retail business structure. The cold chain is a logistics concept, even if ice cream shops may use one.

rw: Fresh fish spoils quickly, so refrigerated transport and storage are essential. A cold chain keeps the product safe and sellable on a long trip across the country.

ww.A long list of advertising slogans for t: Slogans are promotional content and do not keep fish fresh. For perishable goods, the logistics must protect quality during shipment.
ww.A large selection of colors for the boxe: Box colors do not protect fresh fish from spoiling. Preserving product quality across the country is the main concern.
ww.A high markup on each fish that is sold: A high markup affects profit but not whether the fish arrives in good condition. Quality preservation matters most for a perishable shipment.

rw: A distributor buys goods from producers and sells them to retailers or businesses, often storing and delivering them. It connects makers with many buyers and takes on logistics.

ww.A firm that makes goods from raw materia: A firm that makes goods from raw materials is a manufacturer. A distributor buys finished goods rather than producing them.
ww.A person who buys goods for personal use: A person buying for personal use is a consumer. Distributors serve retailers and businesses rather than being the end user.
ww.A group that sets standards for an indus: A group that sets industry standards and issues licenses is a trade or regulatory body. It does not buy and resell goods.

rw: An agent or broker arranges sales for a fee or commission without taking ownership of the goods. This differs from wholesalers and retailers, who buy and own inventory.

ww.A manufacturer who sells only through it: A manufacturer selling through its own channels uses a direct channel and needs no agent. Agents act as middlemen for other firms' products.
ww.A retailer who sells directly to the pub: A retailer sells directly to the public and usually owns the goods it sells. An agent does not take title to the products.
ww.A wholesaler who buys and stores large q: A wholesaler buys and stores goods in large quantities for resale, so it owns the inventory. An agent or broker does not.

rw: A distributor already has relationships and delivery systems for those stores. Using one lets a small brewer reach many states without building its own sales force.

ww.Raise prices until the stores call and a: Raising prices does not create demand or help reach stores. A brewer without a sales team needs a way to be sold, not a higher price.
ww.Wait for stores to find the brewery by p: Waiting for chance discovery is not a strategy and would give slow, unreliable growth across several states. The brewer needs an active channel.
ww.Sell only at its own taproom door to wal: Selling only at its taproom limits reach to walk-in guests. The goal is stores in several states, which a taproom cannot supply.

rw: In a franchise, independent owners sell the franchisor's products or services under its brand name and rules, in return for fees. This expands distribution with the owners' own capital.

ww.A store owned by the producer's employee: A store owned by a producer's employees is an employee-owned or company store. Franchisees are independent owners, not the employees of the producer.
ww.A government-run store that sells goods: A government-run store with fixed prices is a state enterprise. Franchises are private businesses that follow a brand's system.
ww.A store that sells only used goods bough: A used-goods store is a secondhand or resale shop. A franchise is defined by licensed brand use and not by selling used goods.

rw: In vendor-managed inventory the supplier monitors the customer's stock levels and refills them. This reduces stockouts and ordering work for the customer.

ww.A policy that bans reorders of stock for: Banning reorders does not describe vendor-managed inventory. In VMI the supplier replenishes stock, so reordering continues but is handled by the supplier.
ww.A system that sets prices for rivals in: Setting prices for rivals is illegal price fixing. VMI is a cooperative inventory arrangement between a supplier and its customer.
ww.A customer that runs the supplier's fact: A customer running the supplier's factory reverses the VMI arrangement. In VMI, the supplier takes responsibility for the customer's inventory.

rw: The snack maker's staff check the store's shelves and restock them, so the supplier manages the customer's inventory. That arrangement is vendor-managed inventory.

ww.A reverse channel plan: A reverse channel moves used goods back from customers. Here the maker is restocking new snacks, which is a forward flow.
ww.Price fixing by competitors: Price fixing is an illegal agreement between competitors. The scenario involves a cooperative supply arrangement between a snack maker and a store.
ww.Disintermediation plan: Disintermediation means removing middlemen. The grocery store remains in the channel here, so the snack maker is only managing its stock.

rw: FOB and similar terms state who pays shipping costs and who bears the risk of loss or damage during transport. They show when ownership responsibility passes to the buyer.

ww.Deciding which employees ship orders and: Choosing which employees ship orders is an internal staffing decision. Shipping terms are contract terms between buyer and seller.
ww.Choosing advertising for a shipment of g: Advertising choices are promotion decisions. Shipping terms such as FOB only set the responsibilities for transport costs and risk.
ww.Setting the color of a shipping box for: Box color is a packaging design choice. Shipping terms such as FOB are about cost and risk, not appearance.

rw: Under FOB shipping point, title and risk pass to the buyer when goods leave the seller's dock. The buyer typically pays freight and handles any claims for damage in transit.

ww.The carrier: The carrier moves the goods but does not own them. Under FOB shipping point, risk transfers to the buyer, with the carrier only transporting for them.
ww.No one: Someone always bears the risk of loss. FOB shipping point assigns it to the buyer once goods leave the seller's dock.
ww.The seller: The seller bears the risk only until goods are loaded at the seller's dock under FOB shipping point. After that the buyer is responsible.

rw: Last-mile delivery is the final leg of moving a product from a local hub or store to the customer's door. It is often the most costly and visible part of shipping.

ww.The step of designing the product for th: Designing a product is a development step at the start, not a delivery step. Last-mile delivery concerns the final movement to the customer.
ww.The first step of moving raw materials t: Moving raw materials to a factory is early supply chain inbound logistics. Last-mile refers to the end of the delivery process.
ww.The step of setting the retail price for: Setting the retail price is a pricing decision. Last-mile delivery is a physical logistics step.

rw: Same-day delivery requires quick local transport, extra drivers and often smaller loads, so last-mile delivery cost rises most. It is the final and most expensive leg of shipping.

ww.Cost of designing the logo: A logo is a branding cost, unaffected by delivery speed. Same-day delivery changes transport and handling expenses.
ww.Cost of staff training only: Staff training is only a small part of costs and does not rise because of speed. Fast local delivery mainly increases transport and handling costs.
ww.Cost of making the product: Production cost does not depend on delivery speed. Same-day delivery affects how the finished goods are brought to the customer.

rw: A warehouse management system is software that tracks stock locations and movements in a warehouse. It helps staff find items, fill orders and keep records accurate.

ww.A system that sets customer prices for g: Setting customer prices is a pricing function, not warehouse software. A WMS manages inventory handling inside the warehouse.
ww.A system that pays employees their wages: Paying wages is handled by payroll software. A WMS concentrates on stock, locations and warehouse activity.
ww.A system that writes advertisements and: Writing advertisements is a promotion task. A warehouse management system has no role in creating slogans or ads.

rw: In cross-docking, goods move directly from incoming trucks to outgoing trucks with little or no storage. This cuts handling, storage costs and delivery time.

ww.Returning goods to the maker for repair: Returning goods for repair or refund is reverse logistics. Cross-docking is about quickly passing goods through a facility toward customers.
ww.Storing goods for many months before sal: Storing goods for months is the opposite of cross-docking, which is designed to avoid storage and move products through quickly.
ww.Selling goods at a loss to clear stock f: Selling goods at a loss to clear stock is a clearance strategy. Cross-docking is a logistics method, not a pricing approach.

rw: Cross-docking moves goods straight from arriving trucks to outgoing shipments with little storage. That cuts the time goods spend in the warehouse.

ww.Ordering far more than needed from suppl: Ordering far more than needed increases inventory and the time goods sit in storage, which is the opposite of the goal.
ww.Storing goods in several buildings acros: Using more buildings spreads inventory and adds handling, so goods stay in storage no faster. It does not shorten storage time.
ww.Holding goods until prices rise again la: Holding goods until prices rise lengthens storage time and ties up money, so it does not shorten time in storage.

rw: Channel power is the ability of one channel member, such as a large retailer, to influence the decisions and actions of other members. It comes from size, information or control of customers.

ww.The speed of a delivery truck on the hig: Truck speed is a transport factor, not power. Channel power is about one member's ability to influence other members.
ww.The electricity used by a warehouse, bil: Electricity used by a warehouse is an operating expense. Channel power refers to influence among channel members, not energy.
ww.The size of a store's parking lot for it: Parking lot size is a facilities detail. It has no connection to influence in a distribution channel.

rw: The giant retailer is able to demand lower prices and threaten to drop the supplier. This ability to influence another channel member is channel power.

ww.Price discrimination between customers: Price discrimination means charging different customers different prices for the same product. Here a retailer pressures its supplier, which is a different situation.
ww.Direct marketing to buyers online: Direct marketing communicates with buyers directly. The scenario shows a retailer forcing terms on a supplier, not marketing to customers.
ww.A reverse channel for old goods: A reverse channel moves used goods back from customers. The retailer is demanding lower prices from a supplier, not returning goods.

rw: Channel partner incentives are rewards such as bonuses, discounts or prizes that motivate resellers to promote, stock and sell a product more actively.

ww.Penalties for selling too much of a prod: Penalties for selling too much would discourage sales, the opposite of incentives. Producers want resellers to sell more.
ww.Fines for late deliveries made by the re: Fines for late deliveries are penalties, not incentives. Incentives reward good performance rather than punish poor performance.
ww.Taxes paid by resellers on the goods tha: Taxes are charged by governments. Incentives come from producers to encourage partner effort, not from taxes on goods.

rw: A bonus paid to stores for eye-level display rewards resellers for supporting the product. That reward is a channel incentive.

ww.A warranty offer: A warranty offers customers repair or replacement of defective goods. A bonus for stores displaying products is paid to resellers instead.
ww.A recall notice: A recall notice informs people of a defective product that must be returned. It has nothing to do with a bonus for display placement.
ww.A tariff on goods: A tariff is a government tax on imported goods. A maker's bonus to stores is a producer-paid incentive, not a tariff.

rw: At a trade show, producers meet buyers and resellers to show products, build relationships and make deals. It is an efficient way to find new channel partners.

ww.Printing labels for shipments sent out b: Printing shipping labels is a warehouse task. A trade show is an event where companies display products to attract buyers.
ww.Counting the stock inside a warehouse on: Counting warehouse stock is an inventory process. Trade shows are marketing events, not stock counts.
ww.Setting the price of products for custom: Setting product prices is a management decision. Trade shows focus on meeting buyers and displaying products rather than setting prices.

rw: Selective distribution uses a moderate number of outlets chosen for fit with the brand image and service. It balances reach with control, as with many appliance or clothing brands.

ww.Using every possible outlet that is open: Using every possible outlet is intensive distribution. Selective distribution limits outlets rather than using them all.
ww.Using only one outlet in a region, so th: Using one outlet in a region is exclusive distribution, which gives maximum brand control. Selective distribution uses more than one.
ww.Using no outlets at all, and selling onl: Using no outlets and selling only by mail or phone is a direct marketing approach. Selective distribution still sells through chosen outlets.

rw: Using a limited number of specialty stores chosen for fit with the brand is selective distribution. It balances reach with image and customer service.

ww.Exclusive distribution: Exclusive distribution gives one outlet sole rights in an area. A brand using several specialty stores uses more than one outlet, so it is not exclusive.
ww.Intensive distribution: Intensive distribution places a product in as many outlets as possible. A limited set of specialty stores is the opposite.
ww.Direct online selling: Direct online selling skips retailers. The brand here uses specialty running stores, so it is selling through intermediaries.

rw: Reverse logistics moves products back from customers for return, repair, resale or recycling. It handles returns efficiently and can recover value from used goods.

ww.Moving products forward to customers fas: Moving products forward to customers faster is normal forward logistics. Reverse logistics runs in the opposite direction.
ww.Running trucks in reverse gear along the: Driving trucks in reverse gear is a literal misreading. The term refers to the backward flow of goods from customers to sellers.
ww.Cutting prices to move old stock out of: Cutting prices to clear stock is a markdown strategy. Reverse logistics concerns returned goods and not price changes.

rw: Collecting used printer cartridges and recycling them moves products backward from customers to the company. That backward flow is a reverse channel.

ww.Mass distribution: Mass distribution means selling widely to the whole market. Collecting used cartridges is a flow of goods back from customers.
ww.Price skimming: Price skimming sets a high price on a new product at launch. It is unrelated to collecting used items.
ww.Direct selling: Direct selling sells products straight to consumers. The scenario describes recovering used products, which is a different flow.

rw: An SLA is a contract that sets the delivery and performance standards, such as on-time rates, that a partner must meet. It makes expectations clear and measurable.

ww.A rule about advertising colors that app: Rules about advertising colors are brand guidelines. An SLA concerns service and performance levels that partners must meet.
ww.A discount for large orders that a suppl: A volume discount is a pricing incentive for large orders. An SLA sets service standards rather than prices.
ww.A tax form for shipping firms, filed eac: A tax form for shipping firms is a government document. An SLA is a business contract between channel partners.

rw: A contract that requires 98 percent of orders delivered on time sets a measurable standard. That is a service level agreement, which defines expected performance.

ww.A price war in retail: A price war is competition through repeated price cuts. The contract described sets delivery performance standards instead.
ww.A trade show invitation: A trade show invitation asks businesses to attend an event. It does not set delivery obligations for suppliers.
ww.A product recall notice: A product recall notice tells buyers to return defective goods. It has no connection to on-time delivery targets.

rw: Evaluating partners regularly confirms they meet sales, service and quality goals. It lets producers reward strong performers and address problems before customers are hurt.

ww.To raise the price of products for no re: Raising prices for no reason would harm partners and customers. Evaluation is about checking performance, not changing prices without cause.
ww.To avoid speaking with partners about th: Avoiding conversations about results defeats the purpose of an evaluation. Reviews involve discussing results and fixing issues with partners.
ww.To remove all partners from the channel: Removing all partners would destroy the channel. Regular evaluation aims to keep good partners and improve or replace only weak ones.

rw: The producer should review performance, then fix the problem with feedback, support or training, or replace the distributor if it fails to improve. This protects customers and sales.

ww.Raise the price paid to the distributor: Raising the price paid to a poorly performing distributor rewards the problem and does nothing to fix late deliveries and lost orders.
ww.Blame the final customers for the late d: Blaming final customers is unfair and solves nothing. The distributor causes the late deliveries, so the producer must address the distributor's performance.
ww.Ignore the problem to keep things simple: Ignoring the problem allows lost orders to continue and hurts customer relationships. Late deliveries need action from the producer.

rw: Observational research collects data by watching how people behave, such as which products they pick up, without asking questions. It records real actions instead of stated opinions.

ww.Reading industry reports written by othe: Reading industry reports is secondary research, using data that others already collected. Observation gathers fresh data directly.
ww.Testing prices on a single product in a: Testing prices in a few stores is an experiment or test market. Observational research does not change conditions, it just watches.
ww.Asking people to fill out long written s: Long written surveys ask people questions, which is survey research. Observation avoids asking and instead watches behavior.

rw: Recording where shoppers walk and pause is watching behavior without asking questions. That is observation, which shows actual shopping patterns in the store.

ww.A focus group: A focus group is a guided discussion with a small group. Recording shopper movement involves watching behavior, not discussion.
ww.A phone survey: A phone survey asks people questions by telephone. The store here simply records what shoppers do.
ww.Desk research: Desk research reviews existing information. The store is gathering new data from watching shoppers, so it is primary research.

rw: An experiment tests a change in one factor, such as price or package, to see its effect on results while keeping other things the same. It shows cause and effect.

ww.Guessing which price customers prefer wi: Guessing without tests is not research. An experiment is a controlled test that gathers evidence about cause and effect.
ww.Counting the number of stores in a regio: Counting stores is a simple data collection task. An experiment changes something to see how it affects results.
ww.Copying a competitor's price exactly, ev: Copying a competitor's price is an imitation tactic. It is not a test designed to measure how a change affects results.

rw: A/B testing shows two versions to different visitors to see which performs better. It is a marketing experiment that compares results to guide decisions.

ww.A census: A census collects data from every member of a population. Showing two page versions to visitors is a test, not a full count.
ww.A focus group: A focus group is a moderated discussion. Showing different versions to different visitors is not a discussion.
ww.A trend report: A trend report summarizes changes over time. It does not compare versions of a page by showing them to visitors.

rw: A customer panel is a group of customers who give feedback over time. It shows how opinions and behavior change and helps test new ideas.

ww.A group of employees who sell products i: Employees who sell products are a sales team. A customer panel is made up of customers, not staff.
ww.A group of suppliers who set prices for: Suppliers who set prices are sellers and not a panel of customers. Customer panels provide feedback, not pricing.
ww.A group of retailers who sign contracts: Retailers who sign contracts with a maker are channel partners. A customer panel consists of customers.

rw: A census collects data from every member of a population. It is complete but can be costly and slow, which is why samples are often used.

ww.A study of a small group chosen at rando: A study of a small random group is a sample survey. A census collects data from the whole population.
ww.A study of a single competitor in the sa: A study of one competitor is a case study or competitive analysis. A census covers every member of a population, not a single firm.
ww.A study of past reports only, with no ne: Studying past reports only uses secondary data. A census collects new data directly from all members.

rw: Samples can be gathered faster and at lower cost than studying everyone. A well chosen sample gives reliable results without the expense of a census.

ww.Samples are always more accurate than an: Samples are not always more accurate. A census has no sampling error, but samples are chosen for speed and cost.
ww.A census is illegal for businesses in mo: A census is not generally illegal for businesses. Samples are used because a census is expensive and slow.
ww.Samples avoid the need to ask any questi: Samples still ask questions, or observe people. A sample just uses a smaller group, so questions are still required.

rw: A margin of error gives the range within which survey results are likely to differ from the true population value. Smaller margins come from larger samples.

ww.The number of questions on a survey that: The number of questions is the survey length. Margin of error measures how much results might differ from the true population value.
ww.The profit a company makes on each produ: Profit as a percent of price is a profit margin, which is a different concept from a survey's margin of error.
ww.The cost of running a survey, including: Survey cost is a budget item. Margin of error describes the statistical accuracy of the results.

rw: With 52% and a 5 point margin, the true value is likely between 47% and 57% (52 - 5 and 52 + 5). The result is an estimate, not an exact figure.

ww.Exactly 52% of all customers prefer the: The poll is a sample, so 52% is an estimate. The margin of error shows that the true value may differ from 52%.
ww.Between 40% and 60% of customers prefer: A 5 point margin gives a range from 47% to 57%, not 40% to 60%. That range would require a margin of 12 points either way.
ww.Nobody prefers the flavor among all cust: A result of 52% with a 5 point margin cannot mean nobody prefers the flavor. The range from 47% to 57% shows many prefer it.

rw: A closed-ended question offers a fixed set of answer choices, such as yes or no or multiple choice. Answers are easy to tabulate and compare.

ww.A question that allows any written answe: A question allowing any written answer is open-ended. Closed-ended questions limit the answers to fixed choices.
ww.A question that no one can ever answer a: Questions that no one can answer would be useless. A closed-ended question can be answered easily by choosing from options.
ww.A question that asks for a long story in: Asking for a long story is an open-ended question. Closed-ended questions have simple, fixed choices.

rw: 'What do you like most about our store?' has no fixed answers, so respondents reply in their own words. That makes it open-ended, giving richer detail.

ww.Are you satisfied with us: yes or no?: Yes or no allows only two answers, so it is closed-ended. Open-ended questions let people respond in their own words.
A 1 to 5 rating offers fixed choices on a scale. That makes it a closed-ended rating scale question.
ww.Do you shop here weekly, monthly or neve: Weekly, monthly or never gives a fixed list of choices. It is a closed-ended multiple choice question.

rw: A rating scale question asks respondents to choose a number on a scale, such as 1 to 5, to show their opinion. It measures degree and is easy to analyze.

ww.A question that asks for a home address: An address and phone number are contact details. A rating scale question asks for an opinion on a numeric scale.
ww.A question that asks for a story about t: A story about the last visit is an open-ended question. Rating scales use numbers rather than free narratives.
ww.A question that asks for a name only, no: Asking for a name is a simple identification question, not a rating. Rating scale questions require choosing a point on a scale.

rw: Data analysis examines data to find patterns and draw conclusions that help make decisions. Marketers use it to understand customers and measure results.

ww.Collecting data without examining it, st: Collecting data without examining it is only data gathering. Analysis requires reviewing the data to learn something from it.
ww.Deleting data to save space on the compa: Deleting data does not produce insight. Analysis examines data to learn from it, not to remove it.
ww.Printing data on paper for the files in: Printing data for filing only stores it. Analysis requires studying the data to find meaning.

rw: If most customers buy on Fridays, scheduling more staff and promotions that day serves them and increases sales. Good analysis leads to practical action.

ww.Stop recording sales and ignore what cus: Ignoring what customers buy wastes useful information. Sales data should be used to guide decisions, not discarded.
ww.Raise prices only on Mondays, as custome: Raising prices only on Mondays does not respond to Friday demand. It is also unrelated to the pattern the data revealed.
ww.Close the store on Fridays to save on st: Closing on Fridays would lose the busiest day of sales. The data shows Friday is the best day to be open.

rw: Sales forecasting estimates future sales using past data, trends and market conditions. Businesses use forecasts to plan inventory, staffing and budgets.

ww.Setting the price of products sold in th: Setting prices is a pricing decision. Sales forecasting predicts future sales and does not set what products cost.
ww.Counting stock in a warehouse at the end: Counting stock is an inventory task. Forecasting looks forward rather than recording what is on hand.
ww.Recording sales that happened in the pas: Recording past sales is bookkeeping. Forecasting uses past sales to predict future sales.

rw: Growth of 10 percent on 800 units is 800 x 0.10 = 80. Adding gives 800 + 80 = 880 units as the forecast.

ww.900 units: 900 units would be 12.5% growth over 800. Ten percent growth means 800 x 0.10 = 80 extra units, so the forecast is 880.
ww.8,000 units: 8,000 units is ten times 800, which would mean 900% growth. A 10 percent increase adds only 80 units to 800.
ww.810 units: 810 units adds 10 units instead of 10 percent. Ten percent of 800 is 80, so the forecast is higher.

rw: A KPI is a measurable value showing how well a marketing goal is being met, such as conversion rate or sales growth. It helps teams track progress and adjust plans.

ww.A description of a brand's colors, fonts: Brand colors and fonts describe visual identity. A KPI measures progress toward a goal in numbers.
ww.A record of employees' birthdays and the: Employee birthdays are personnel records. They do not measure marketing results.
ww.A list of competitors and the prices the: A list of competitors is market information. A KPI is a measurable value tied to an objective, and not a list of rivals.

rw: Conversion rate is the share of people reached who take the desired action, such as buying or signing up. It shows how effective marketing is at turning interest into results.

ww.The number of employees hired by the fir: Employee hiring counts are a human resources number. Conversion rate measures customers taking an action.
ww.The rate at which a currency changes int: Currency exchange rates describe money changing between currencies. A marketing conversion rate measures customer actions.
ww.The speed of a website when it loads on: Website load speed is a performance measure. It does not describe the share of visitors who take an action.

rw: Conversion rate is buyers divided by people reached: 50 / 1,000 = 0.05, or 5%. This shows the share of viewers who took the desired action.

ww.50%: 50% would mean 500 of the 1,000 people bought. Only 50 bought, which is a much smaller share.
ww.20%: 20% would require 200 buyers out of 1,000. With 50 buyers, 50 / 1,000 gives a lower rate.
ww.0.5%: 0.5% would be 5 buyers per 1,000 people. The 50 buyers make 5%, so the decimal point is misplaced.

rw: ROMI measures profit gained from marketing relative to what was spent. A positive ROMI shows marketing creates more value than it costs.

ww.The size of a marketing team and the pay: Team size and pay are staffing details. ROMI compares marketing returns to marketing spending.
ww.The cost of one advertisement placed in: The cost of one ad is a single expense. ROMI compares total return with total investment.
ww.The total number of ads shown, counted b: Counting ads shown is a reach or impression metric. It does not measure financial return.

rw: Net gain is the return minus the cost: $5,000 - $2,000 = $3,000. This treats the $5,000 as the return from the campaign and subtracts what was spent.

ww.$7,000: $7,000 adds the cost to the profit ($2,000 + $5,000). The net gain subtracts the cost from the return rather than adding.
ww.$5,000: $5,000 is the stated return before subtracting the $2,000 spent. Net gain accounts for the campaign cost, so it must be lower.
ww.$2,500: $2,500 would come from dividing $5,000 by 2, which is not how net gain is found. Subtract the $2,000 cost from the $5,000 return.

rw: Behavioral segmentation groups customers by how they buy and use products, such as purchase frequency, brand loyalty or usage rate. It helps tailor offers to each group.

ww.Grouping customers alphabetically by the: Alphabetical grouping by name sorts a list but says nothing about buying behavior. Behavioral segmentation uses actions.
ww.Grouping customers by the color of their: Clothing color has no relation to how people buy or use products, so it does not form a useful segment.
ww.Grouping customers by the day they were: Birth day alone is not behavior. Behavioral segmentation uses actions such as purchase frequency or loyalty.

rw: Offers aimed at customers who have not bought in six months target a segment based on buying behavior. That is behavior-based segmentation used to win them back.

ww.Channel conflict among sellers: Channel conflict is a dispute between channel members. Sending offers to lapsed customers is a marketing action, not a dispute.
ww.Price fixing among competitors: Price fixing is an illegal agreement among competitors. A store offering deals to its own customers is not that.
ww.Mass marketing to everyone equally: Mass marketing sends the same message to everyone. The store selected a specific group of customers, so this is targeted.

rw: Market research ethics means honest, fair treatment of participants and their data, with consent and privacy protected. It keeps trust and ensures reliable findings.

ww.Selling personal data to anyone who want: Selling personal data to anyone is a privacy violation. Research ethics protects participants and their information.
ww.Changing results to look better for the: Changing results to please a client is data manipulation. Ethical research reports findings honestly.
ww.Collecting data without telling people,: Collecting data without telling people breaks the principle of informed consent. Ethical research tells participants what is collected.

rw: Altering survey results to please a client is unethical manipulation. It misleads decision makers and violates professional research standards.

ww.A sampling technique for surveys: Sampling is a method of choosing respondents. Changing results is not a sampling technique at all.
ww.A normal practice in research: Manipulating results is not normal practice. Professional codes of conduct forbid altering findings.
ww.A way to protect user privacy: Changing results does not protect privacy. Privacy protection involves safeguarding participant information, which is a different matter.

rw: Loyalty cards record what members buy and how often. This purchase data helps stores understand habits and tailor offers.

ww.Replacing all surveys, as purchases show: Purchase data does not replace surveys because it shows what people buy but not why. Surveys reveal opinions and motives.
ww.Raising prices for members who have a lo: A loyalty card is meant to reward customers, not to increase their prices. Raising prices for members would defeat its purpose.
ww.Hiding what customers buy from the store: Loyalty card data goes to the store, which uses it to learn about customers. It does not hide purchases from the owner.

rw: Buying diapers and baby food suggests a family with a baby. Sending relevant baby product offers meets real needs and is likely to produce sales.

ww.Send offers for totally unrelated items: Offers for unrelated items would waste money and miss the shopper's needs. The data points to baby products.
ww.Stop sending any offers to the shopper: Stopping offers wastes an opportunity. The data shows what the shopper wants and should be used to help them.
ww.Share the data publicly on a website: Posting customer data publicly violates privacy and may break laws. Customer data should be kept secure and used responsibly.

rw: Syndicated data is market data collected by a research firm and sold to many clients. Examples include retail audits and TV ratings, which save each client the cost of collecting it.

ww.Data with no source that anyone can read: Syndicated data is not free and without a source. It is collected by a research firm and sold to clients.
ww.Data that is secret and kept inside one: Secret data kept in one company is proprietary internal data. Syndicated data is shared with many paying clients.
ww.Data collected by one company for its ow: Data collected by one company for its own use is primary research. Syndicated data is sold to multiple clients.

rw: A competitive intelligence report summarizes information about rivals' products, prices and plans. It helps a firm respond to competitors and spot opportunities, using legal sources.

ww.A list of employee names and the jobs th: A list of employee names is a staff directory. A competitive intelligence report focuses on rivals.
ww.A summary of the company's own profit an: A summary of the company's own profit is a financial report. Competitive intelligence studies other firms.
ww.A report of a store's opening hours and: Store hours are basic business details. A competitive report analyzes rivals' strategy.

rw: Studying a rival's public price list and ads uses existing, publicly available information. That is secondary competitive information and is legal and ethical to collect.

ww.Primary survey data it gathered: Primary survey data is collected directly by the firm. A rival's public price list already exists, so this is not primary data.
ww.Confidential data from the rival: A rival's public price list and ads are open to anyone, so the data is not confidential. Confidential data would be hidden from the public.
ww.Stolen trade secrets of the rival: Public prices and ads are not trade secrets. Trade secrets are confidential information, and taking them would be illegal.

rw: A dealer network is a group of independent businesses authorized to sell a maker's products. Car and equipment makers use dealers to reach local customers.

ww.A group of workers who deliver a maker's: Workers delivering products are a delivery staff. A dealer network is a group of independent sellers.
ww.A group of competitors who set prices to: Competitors who set prices together would be breaking antitrust laws. A dealer network is a channel structure.
ww.A group of customers who review products: Customers who review products are reviewers. Dealers are businesses that sell a maker's products.

rw: Selling through independently owned dealerships places intermediaries between the maker and the buyer. That is an indirect channel using dealers.

ww.A cold chain for perishable goods: A cold chain handles perishable goods. A car maker selling through dealers is a distribution arrangement.
ww.A reverse channel for old cars: A reverse channel moves used goods back from customers. The car maker is selling new vehicles forward.
ww.A direct channel selling to buyers: A direct channel sells straight to buyers. Using independent dealerships means the maker sells through intermediaries.

rw: An SKU is a unique code that identifies a specific product, including its size or color, for inventory tracking. It lets stores count and reorder each variation accurately.

ww.A price tag on a shelf that shows the co: A price tag shows cost. An SKU is a code that identifies a product variant for inventory.
ww.A tax code for imported goods used at th: A tax code for imports is a customs classification. An SKU is used inside a business for inventory.
ww.A slogan for a product that is used in t: A slogan is a promotional phrase. An SKU is a code and has no advertising purpose.

rw: Each size and color combination is a separate SKU, so 3 sizes x 4 colors = 12 SKUs. This lets the store track each variation of the shirt.

ww.1: One would only count the shirt as a single item. Each size and color combination has its own SKU, so there are 12.
ww.7: 7 comes from adding 3 and 4. Variants combine, so sizes and colors are multiplied to give 12.
ww.34: 34 comes from writing 3 and 4 side by side. SKUs are found by multiplying the options: 3 x 4 = 12.

rw: Safety stock is extra inventory kept to avoid running out during supplier delays or demand surges. It protects sales and customer service at the cost of some storage.

ww.Stock that is about to expire within the: Stock about to expire is perishable inventory. Safety stock is extra inventory held as a buffer.
ww.Stock that has been recalled by the make: Recalled stock is defective and must be removed. Safety stock is good extra inventory kept as a buffer.
ww.Inventory kept for safety inspections on: Safety stock is not for inspections. It serves as a buffer against shortages, and the goods are available for sale.

rw: Holding safety stock gives a buffer when the supplier is late or demand spikes. It prevents stockouts and lost sales.

ww.Dropping the supplier: Dropping the supplier does not solve a demand spike and may create a new problem. A buffer of inventory is a better fix.
ww.Ordering less, no buffer: Ordering less without a buffer increases the risk of running out when the supplier is late or demand rises.
ww.Ignoring forecasts: Ignoring forecasts removes planning information and makes stockouts more likely. A safety stock covers uncertainty that forecasts cannot.

rw: A data privacy notice tells customers what data is collected, why, and how it is used and protected. It supports transparency and legal compliance.

ww.A list of customers' credit card numbers: A list of card numbers is sensitive data that must be protected. A privacy notice informs customers about data use and does not publish it.
ww.A report of a company's yearly profit th: A yearly profit report is a financial document for owners. A privacy notice is addressed to customers about their data.
ww.A discount code for loyal buyers that is: A discount code is a promotion. A privacy notice explains data practices and does not offer deals.

rw: A clear privacy notice explains how collected emails will be used. This gives visitors transparency and helps meet legal requirements.

ww.A countdown timer for sales shown on the: A countdown timer is a sales gimmick. It does not explain why emails are collected.
ww.A larger logo at the top of the page for: A larger logo changes the design. It does nothing to tell visitors why their emails are collected.
ww.A new background color for the home page: A new background color changes appearance only. The site needs a notice explaining its use of email data.

rw: A cookie is a small file stored on a visitor's device to remember activity, such as logins or items in a cart. Websites use cookies to personalize and analyze visits.

ww.A snack offered to site visitors who fil: A snack offered to visitors is a literal cookie. In web terms it is a data file.
ww.A password for the site that a visitor c: A password is a login credential. A cookie is a small file that stores browsing information.
ww.A coupon sent by email to a visitor of t: A coupon sent by email is a promotion. A web cookie is stored on the visitor's device.

rw: Sites explain that they collect data through cookies and obtain consent where laws such as GDPR require it. This respects visitors' privacy choices.

ww.To hide the privacy policy from the peop: Cookie notices do not hide a privacy policy. They are meant to inform visitors about data collection.
ww.To collect payment from visitors before: Accepting cookies is not a payment. It is a consent step about data use.
ww.To reduce the speed of the site, as each: Cookies do not mainly slow the site. The prompt exists for privacy transparency, not performance.

rw: A dashboard displays key marketing numbers at a glance, such as visits, sales and conversion rate. It helps managers see performance and make decisions quickly.

ww.A tool that sets prices for each of the: Setting prices is a pricing task. A dashboard displays data and does not set prices.
ww.A printed list of competitors posted on: A printed competitor list is a document. A dashboard is a live display of the company's own key metrics.
ww.A file that stores customer passwords in: Storing passwords is a security function. A dashboard presents marketing metrics rather than credentials.

rw: Checking web visits, sales and email results each morning monitors performance. This lets the manager spot problems early and react before they grow.

ww.Replacing market research, as dashboards: Dashboards show performance data but not buyer motives. They cannot replace market research, which explains why people buy.
ww.Hiding results from the team and the oth: A dashboard shares results with the team rather than hiding them. Its purpose is visibility.
ww.Setting employees' pay for the whole yea: Pay is set by compensation plans. A dashboard monitors results and does not set salaries.

rw: A conversion funnel maps the steps a customer takes from awareness to purchase. The numbers narrow at each step, which shows where marketing loses prospects.

ww.A tool for pouring liquids into bottles: A funnel for pouring liquids is a literal tool. In marketing it is a model of customer steps.
ww.A rule about shipping times and delivery: Shipping times and delivery dates are logistics terms. A conversion funnel describes customer stages.
ww.A list of products on sale at the front: A list of products on sale is a display or catalog. A conversion funnel tracks customer progress toward buying.

rw: Net pay, or take-home pay, equals gross pay minus taxes and other deductions. Gross pay is the full amount earned before anything is withheld from the paycheck.

ww.Net pay is the amount before any deducti: This reverses the definitions. Gross pay is the amount before deductions, so net pay is the lower amount left after deductions are taken out.
ww.They are always equal in value for every: Gross and net pay are rarely equal, since taxes and other deductions are subtracted from gross pay. Only a worker with no deductions would see equal amounts.
ww.Gross pay is net pay minus taxes and oth: This reverses the relationship. Net pay is gross pay minus deductions, not the other way around, because gross pay is the larger figure.
